translations.text: God's church, which after Christ's passion had been living in that city under James the Righteous, left the city all together for a town by the river Jordan;

and then they were besieged from outside by the Roman army for so long that many thousands there died of hunger. Because there were so many, they could not be buried, so the bodies were thrown over the wall.
Some, however, wanted to bury them out of love for their kin, but they soon died of weakness.
Of the boys who were under sixteen years old, they sent ninety thousand away to various nations as slaves, and nothing of that accursed race remained in the land.
The temple was consecrated to God, for his services and hymns of praise and for the prayers of the faithful; but the greedy high priests allowed trading to be carried on inside it.
…living within the temple, received the people's offerings with pretended holiness, and persecuted those who came to the temple without an offering.
…would not withhold his teaching from the perverse Jews, because there were many good people among the wicked who were improved by that teaching, even though the perverse ones opposed it.
He also confirmed the teaching with miracles, so that the chosen would be all the more faithful,
and the reprobate would have no excuse, because they refused to believe in the true Saviour either through divine signs or through living teaching.
Now the blessed Gregory says that their destruction bears some likeness to every perverse person who delights in evil deeds and rejoices in the worst things.
The merciful Lord, who then mourned the doomed citizens with tears, grieves daily over such people.
But if they knew of the downfall that is coming upon them, they would mourn for themselves with a sorrowful voice.
Truly, this following saying applies to the soul that is perishing: "Today you live in peace, but the vengeance to come is now hidden from your eyes."
The soul has peace in its day when it refuses to weaken its present pleasure with any worry about future misfortune, and goes with its eyes shut to the fire of punishment.
…because it is in great conflict with itself over why it would not, while still alive, take any care to foresee the downfall that it then suffers.
The devils show the sinful soul its evil thoughts, its harmful words and its wicked deeds, and torment it with many kinds of threats,
Its children fall in death when the unlawful thoughts it now conceives are utterly destroyed in the final vengeance,
as the psalmist sang about this: "Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the children of men, in whom there is no salvation.
Their spirit departs, and they return to the earth, and on that day all their thoughts perish."
Truly, it follows in the gospel: "And they will not leave in you one stone upon another."
When the perverse mind heaps evil upon evil and perversity upon perversity, what does it do but, as it were, lay stone upon stone?
But when the soul is led to its punishment, then the whole building of its scheming is thrown down, because it did not recognize the time of its visitation.
In many ways Almighty God visits the souls of men: sometimes with teaching, sometimes with miracles, sometimes with sicknesses;
…but if it ignores these visitations, then at its end it will be handed over for eternal punishment to the fiends whom it obeyed in life through grave sins.
Then those who earlier enticed it into sins with various desires will be its tormentors in the torment of hell.
The Lord went into the temple and drove out the traders with a whip. The traders within the temple signified unrighteous teachers in God's church.
Oxen, sheep, and doves were sold there, and money-changers sat there.

The ox tills for its lord, and the teacher sells oxen in God's church if he carries out his lord's tilling, that is, if he preaches the gospel to those under him for earthly gain and not for divine love.

He traffics in sheep if he seeks the praise of foolish men for his pious works. Of such the Saviour said, "They have received the reward of their works"; that is, the fame of empty praise that was pleasing to them.
The teacher is a seller of doves who will not use the gift that God gave him without his deserving it for the benefit of other men without payment;
as Christ himself taught: "Without price you received the gift; give it to others without price."
He who with feigned holiness labours for himself in God's church and cares nothing for Christ's tilling is without doubt counted a money-changer.
But the Saviour drives such merchants out of his house when he condemns them and cuts them off from the fellowship of his chosen.
"My house is a house of prayer, and you have made it a den of thieves."
It happens very often that the perverse come to high rank in God's church, and then by their wickedness they spiritually slay those under them, whom they ought to bring to life with their prayers.
What are such men but thieves? The mind of every believing person is God's house, as the apostle said: "God's temple is holy, which you are."
But that mind is not a house of prayer but a den of thieves if it loses the innocence and simplicity of true holiness and with perverse thoughts plots harm to others.
"And he was teaching daily in the temple."
Christ then taught the people in his presence, and he now daily teaches the minds of believing people with divine teaching, by careful thought, so that they may shun evil and do good.
It is not complete for the believer to cease from evil unless he does good.
The blessed Gregory said, "My brothers, I would like to tell you a little story, which can greatly edify your minds, if you will listen to it with attention.
There was a nobly born man in the province of Valeria named Chrysaorius, who was as greatly filled with sins as he was enriched with earthly wealth.
He was puffed up with pride, and subject to his fleshly lusts, and inflamed with immoderate greed.
But when God purposed to put an end to his wickedness, he fell sick and was brought to the point of death.

Then at the very hour when he was to die, he looked up, and black spirits stood around him and pressed upon him with great menace, so that they might seize his soul at his departure and take it with them to the prisons of hell.
He then began to tremble and turn pale and to sweat beyond measure, and with a great outcry to beg for a respite, and his son Maximus, whom I afterwards saw as a monk,
but with this outcry the black fiends drew the soul out of the body and led it away."
Lo, what did it profit him that he saw the black spirits at his departure, when he could not have the respite that he desired?
You, Almighty Lord, have mercy on us sinners, and so order our departure that, with our sins atoned for, after this perilous life we may be joined in fellowship with your saints.
